rv.q: The opera is a triumph of drama on every level.
Kaija Saariaho's 'Innocence,' one of the most important new operas of this century, finally made it to the Metropolitan Opera on Monday in a superb performance.
Despite its beauty and power, the Met’s Innocence had me wanting to run.
Innocence is not an easy, relaxing night at the opera.
He certainly took her ideas and ran with them, in a brilliantly conceived concoction.
And color, above all, is central to Saariaho’s musical language.

At the Metropolitan Opera, Innocence proves a gripping and perhaps divisive piece which feels real because it is a reflection of our reality, with no realistic hope of finding peace. Saariaho's score likewise seems to turn continuously in an elongated line.
It is a small, intimate work that in its coolly incandescent way, burrows its way into the listener’s mind and heart.
The entire ensemble worked together seamlessly to create an experience that I won't soon forget.
But as it is, Innocence is the kind of opera the public maybe doesn’t know that it needs.

cn.t: Saariaho's harrowing final opera about a school shooting earns strong praise for its musical power and emotional impact, though some critics find the difficult subject matter nearly overwhelming despite the work's undeniable artistry.
